mcqs.question: A classifier predicts "fraud" for a transaction that was actually fraudulent. This is counted as a:
options: True positive
False positive
True negative
False negative
mcqs.explanation: Predicted positive and actually positive is a true positive by definition. A false positive would be predicting fraud on a legitimate transaction; true/false negative both involve predicting "not fraud", which didn't happen here.

mcqs.question: A hospital dataset has 2% positive (disease) cases. A model that always predicts "no disease" achieves what accuracy and recall?
options: 98% accuracy, 98% recall
98% accuracy, 0% recall
2% accuracy, 100% recall
50% accuracy, 50% recall
mcqs.explanation: Always predicting the majority class gets accuracy equal to the majority class's share (98%), but since it never predicts positive, it catches zero true positives, giving 0% recall. This is exactly why accuracy alone is misleading on imbalanced data.

mcqs.question: A spam filter is tuned to almost never flag real email as spam, even if it means more spam reaches the inbox. This filter is optimizing for:
options: High recall, accepting lower precision
High accuracy only
High precision, accepting lower recall
Low false positives and low false negatives simultaneously
mcqs.explanation: Minimizing real email flagged as spam means minimizing false positives, which is what precision protects against. Recall would mean catching more spam even at the cost of more false alarms — the opposite goal here. Option D describes an outcome the precision/recall trade-off makes impossible to guarantee at once.

mcqs.question: For a cancer-screening model, why might a team choose F2 over F1 as their headline metric?
options: F2 is mathematically always higher than F1, making the model look better
F2 is easier to compute and doesn't require a confusion matrix
F2 ignores precision entirely, simplifying the calculation
F2 weights recall more heavily, matching the higher cost of missing a real case
mcqs.explanation: F-beta lets you weight recall against precision by the real cost ratio; F2 weights recall twice as heavily, fitting a domain where misses are far costlier than false alarms. F2 isn't systematically higher (A is false), still incorporates precision (C is false), and is computed from the same confusion matrix as F1 (D is false).

mcqs.question: On a dataset with 0.5% positive class, a model achieves ROC-AUC of 0.95 but PR-AUC of only 0.30. What does this gap most likely indicate?
options: The model has many false positives relative to true positives, which the huge true-negative count masks in ROC-AUC
The ROC-AUC calculation has a bug
PR-AUC is miscalibrated for imbalanced data and should be ignored
The model is performing very well overall and the two numbers don't actually conflict
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic ROC-AUC blind spot on rare-positive data: false positive rate stays tiny because the true-negative count is huge, so ROC-AUC looks great even while precision — and therefore PR-AUC — is poor. Options A and C dismiss a real and well-documented signal, and D ignores that the two metrics are telling meaningfully different stories here.

mcqs.question: A 10-class classifier completely fails on one rare class that makes up 2% of the data, while performing well on the other nine. Which averaging scheme will most clearly expose this failure in the reported F1 score?
options: Weighted-average F1, since it accounts for all classes
Macro-average F1, since it weights every class equally regardless of frequency, so the rare class's 0% score pulls the average down sharply
Both will show an identical drop, since they measure the same underlying errors
Neither — averaging always hides per-class failures
mcqs.explanation: Weighted-average scales each class's contribution by its frequency, so a class that's only 2% of the data barely moves the overall number even at 0% recall — the failure gets diluted away. Macro-average treats every class as equally important regardless of size, so that same 0% score contributes its full, undiluted share to the average, making the failure visible instead of hidden.
